title: Can You Outsmart AI?
description: A highly interactive 75-minute AI literacy experience built around context, verification, human judgment, and an earned Human in the Loop finale.

steps.label: ARRIVAL
steps.title: Can You Outsmart AI?
steps.lead: AI literacy is not about access. It is about judgment.
steps.studentTask: Join on your phone, then look up.

runbook.openWith: Before I tell you who I am, I want to know something about you.
runbook.landHere: This is an experience, not a lecture.
runbook.transition: Make the first decision before I explain anything.

steps.label: TRUST AI?
steps.title: Would you trust AI with a decision that could cost you money?
steps.studentTask: Vote before you hear anyone else.

runbook.openWith: No discussion yet. I want your first instinct.
runbook.ask: Would you trust AI with a decision that could cost you money?
runbook.revealWhen: Most of the room has voted.
runbook.landHere: Trust is not binary. Consequence changes the standard.
runbook.transition: Now let’s name what AI is actually doing.

steps.label: MINIMUM MODEL
steps.title: Everyone will use AI. Your advantage is judgment.
steps.lead: AI predicts patterns, responds to context, and can sound confident when it is wrong.
steps.studentTask: Phone down. Listen for the three ideas you will use for the rest of the session.
steps.roomInstruction: PREDICTS · RESPONDS TO CONTEXT · CAN BE CONFIDENTLY WRONG

runbook.openWith: I am not going to teach you transformers. You need three ideas.
runbook.whyMatters: Gives students the minimum mental model needed for the challenges.
runbook.landHere: AI can be useful without being authoritative.
runbook.transition: Challenge one: what happens when the context changes?

steps.label: CHALLENGE 1
steps.title: Help me survive my first semester.
steps.lead: What does the AI need to know before this prompt becomes useful?
steps.studentTask: Turn to 2–3 people. Name what is missing before anyone asks AI.

runbook.openWith: Do not fix the wording yet. Tell me what the AI does not know.
runbook.ask: What would change what ‘good advice’ means?
runbook.pause: 60 seconds with a neighbor, then call out answers.
runbook.listenFor: Who, goal, schedule, work, commute, anxiety, resources, constraints.
runbook.ifQuiet: Ask: would the same advice work for a commuter working 25 hours?
runbook.landHere: The problem is not magic wording. It is missing context.
runbook.transition: Watch the answer change while the AI stays the same.

steps.label: CONTEXT EXPERIMENT
steps.title: Same AI. Different world.
steps.lead: Add one piece of context at a time and watch what ‘good advice’ becomes.
steps.studentTask: After each reveal, say what should change in the advice.
steps.roomInstruction: WHAT CHANGED? · WHY SHOULD THE ANSWER CHANGE?

runbook.openWith: I am keeping the AI constant. I am changing the situation.
runbook.ask: What advice becomes more useful now? What becomes less useful?
runbook.listenFor: Time constraints, access, energy, social support, communication style.
runbook.pushFurther: Which piece of context changed the answer the most?
runbook.landHere: Context changes what a useful answer looks like.

steps.label: FRAMEWORK
steps.title: You just discovered the framework.
steps.lead: WHO → GOAL → SITUATION → CONSTRAINTS → OUTPUT → CHECK
steps.studentTask: Pick the one element you most often forget when using AI.
steps.roomInstruction: WHO · GOAL · SITUATION · CONSTRAINTS · OUTPUT · CHECK

runbook.openWith: I did not give you this framework first because I wanted you to feel the problem.
runbook.whyMatters: Names the transferable structure after students discover it.
runbook.ask: Which element do you usually leave out?
runbook.landHere: Better context improves usefulness; CHECK protects you from confident mistakes.
runbook.transition: Now the harder problem: what if the answer looks good?

steps.label: CHALLENGE 2
steps.title: Would you trust this answer?
steps.studentTask: Read the answer and commit before the reveal.

runbook.openWith: This answer is mostly sensible. That is what makes this difficult.
runbook.pause: Give enough time to read; do not hint at the trap.
runbook.listenFor: Students reacting to tone versus evidence.
runbook.landHere: A mostly good answer can still contain one costly error.
runbook.transition: Now hunt for what deserves verification.

steps.label: GHOST HUNT
steps.title: Find the ghosts.
steps.studentTask: Choose the TWO things you would verify first before acting.
steps.roomInstruction: WHICH TWO CREATE THE HIGHEST VERIFICATION BURDEN?

runbook.openWith: The deadline on the previous slide was fabricated for this exercise.
runbook.ask: Which two claims would you verify first—and why those two?
runbook.pause: Vote, then discuss with a neighbor.
runbook.ifTheySay: Everything should be checked → ask what deserves the highest priority first.
runbook.pushFurther: Would your verification standard change if the consequence were money, grades, health, or safety?
runbook.landHere: Fluency is not evidence. Verification rises with consequence.
runbook.transition: But AI literacy is not learning to distrust AI.

steps.label: DEBRIEF
steps.title: AI literacy ≠ distrust.
steps.lead: It means knowing what deserves trust.
steps.studentTask: Phone down. Reconcile two truths: AI can be useful, and AI can be wrong.

runbook.openWith: If you leave thinking ‘AI is bad,’ I failed.
runbook.whyMatters: Prevents the session from collapsing into generic AI skepticism.
runbook.ask: What made the previous answer useful even though one claim was fabricated?
runbook.listenFor: General guidance, questions to ask, comparison structure, low-stakes support.
runbook.landHere: The skill is calibrated trust, not blanket trust or blanket distrust.
runbook.transition: So where is AI genuinely excellent?

steps.label: POSITIVE SURPRISE
steps.title: AI can be excellent at low-stakes support.
steps.lead: Explain differently. Generate practice. Brainstorm options. Compare drafts.
steps.studentTask: Call out one task where AI has genuinely helped you learn or work.

runbook.openWith: Give AI credit where it earns it.
runbook.ask: Where has AI actually made you better—not just faster?
runbook.landHere: Low-stakes support is different from high-stakes authority.
runbook.transition: Now decide who should own the decision.

steps.label: HUMAN OVERRIDE
steps.title: Who owns the decision?
steps.lead: AI DECIDES · AI HELPS · HUMAN DECIDES
steps.studentTask: You are about to make three calls. Reasonable people can disagree.
steps.roomInstruction: AI DECIDES · AI HELPS · HUMAN DECIDES

runbook.openWith: These are not trick questions. I care about your boundary and your reasoning.
runbook.landHere: The question is not ‘Can AI do it?’ It is ‘Who should own the consequence?’

steps.label: HUMAN OVERRIDE · 1
steps.title: AI summarizes a university policy before you act.
steps.studentTask: Choose who should own the decision.

runbook.listenFor: Summarization can help; official source still matters.
runbook.landHere: AI can reduce reading burden without becoming the authority.

steps.label: HUMAN OVERRIDE · 2
steps.title: AI recommends which course you should take next semester.
steps.studentTask: Choose, then be ready to defend the boundary.

runbook.ask: What context would AI need? What could happen if it is wrong?
runbook.listenFor: Prerequisites, degree progress, goals, schedule, advisor knowledge.
runbook.landHere: AI can surface options; the student and qualified humans own the decision.
runbook.transition: Now move beyond your own consequences.

steps.label: HUMAN OVERRIDE · 3
steps.title: AI screens job applicants and ranks who deserves interviews.
steps.studentTask: Choose. Then ask who bears the consequence if the system is biased or wrong.

runbook.ask: Who is affected by a bad decision here?
runbook.pushFurther: Does efficiency justify delegating the judgment?
runbook.landHere: The consequence belongs to humans even when AI contributes.
runbook.transition: Turn that into one rule you will actually use.

steps.label: TRANSFER
steps.title: The next time I use AI, I will ______.
steps.lead: Make it specific enough that you could actually do it.
steps.studentTask: Write one sentence: what will you do differently after today?
steps.roomInstruction: ONE RULE YOU WILL ACTUALLY USE

runbook.openWith: This is the most important answer you give today.
runbook.ask: What will you actually do differently?
runbook.pause: 2 minutes to write, then reveal a few anonymous responses.
runbook.listenFor: More context, verification, asking for uncertainty, checking policy, keeping human judgment.
runbook.landHere: AI literacy should change behavior, not just vocabulary.
runbook.transition: You have been doing one thing all hour: staying human in the loop.

steps.label: FINALE
steps.title: You’ve been the Human in the Loop.
steps.studentTask: When I say go, open the Human in the Loop experience and take your optional photo.
steps.roomInstruction: HUMAN IN THE LOOP · AI CAN GENERATE. I DECIDE.
steps.actionLabel: Open Human in the Loop photo →

runbook.openWith: You have spent the last hour deciding what AI should do—and what should stay human.
runbook.whyMatters: Turns the learning identity into a memorable optional artifact.
runbook.ask: If you want it, claim the badge. Your photo stays on your device.
runbook.pause: Give students time to take/save the photo.
runbook.landHere: The artifact represents a judgment skill, not just a cool AI trick.

steps.label: CLOSE
steps.title: AI can generate. AI can recommend. You own the consequence.
steps.studentTask: Phone down. Take the final idea with you.

runbook.openWith: AI can generate. AI can recommend. You own the consequence.
runbook.pause: Let the line sit before speaking again.
